roadmap.title: Knowledge Check

props.subtitle: Reuse responses safely so pages load fast and servers stay calm.
props.title: HTTP Caching

bullets: The Cache-Control header tells caches what they may store and for how long
Shared caches (CDNs) and private caches (browsers) follow different rules
what.summary: HTTP caching lets a browser or CDN keep a copy of a response and reuse it instead of asking the origin server again.

why.impact: A correct caching policy can remove most repeat traffic from your servers.
why.summary: Every request that hits the origin costs latency and compute.

categories.analogy: Like milk with a best-before date.
categories.description: The response may be reused without contacting the server until it is N seconds old.
categories.details: Use long max-age values for fingerprinted static assets such as app.3f9a.js.
categories.subtitle: Fresh for N seconds
categories.title: max-age

categories.analogy: Like calling ahead to confirm a reservation before driving over.
categories.description: Caches may store the response but must check with the server before every reuse.
categories.details: Good for HTML documents that change often but benefit from cheap 304 Not Modified replies.
outOfScope: Secrets that must never touch disk
categories.subtitle: Store, but revalidate first
categories.title: no-cache

categories.analogy: Like a shredder: read it once, then it is gone.
categories.description: No cache may store any part of the response.
categories.details: Use for banking pages and other sensitive data.
categories.subtitle: Never keep a copy
categories.title: no-store

categories.analogy: Like a diary: you may keep it, the library may not.
categories.description: Only the user's own browser cache may store the response; shared caches such as CDNs must not.
categories.details: Use for personalized pages like a logged-in dashboard.
categories.subtitle: Browser only, not CDNs
categories.title: private

choices.explanation: Correct. private allows only the user's own browser cache to store the response.
max-age sets a freshness lifetime but does not stop shared caches from storing it.
no-store forbids every cache, including the browser, from keeping a copy.

questions.hint: Think about shared vs private caches.
questions.question: A logged-in dashboard is different for every user. Which directive stops a CDN from storing it while still letting the browser cache it?

choices.explanation: no-store prevents storage entirely, so there is nothing to revalidate.
Correct. no-cache stores the response but revalidates before every reuse.
A long max-age would serve stale HTML without checking the server.

questions.question: Your HTML changes often, but you want cheap 304 replies. Which directive fits?
